name: ZKsync
rootCause: The ZKsync security team discovered that an admin account had been compromised, giving the hacker control of approximately $5 million worth of ZK tokens — the remaining unclaimed tokens from the ZKsync airdrop. The ZKsync Security Council sent an onchain message to the hacker on Monday, April 21st at 15:03 UTC. In an effort to resolve this matter in the spirit of safe harbor, they offered a 10% bounty for returning 90% of the funds involved in the exploit. On Wednesday, April 23rd at 14:39 UTC, 90% of the funds were returned to the Era and Ethereum L1 addresses controlled by the Security Council.

descriptions.text: The ZKsync security team discovered that an admin account had been compromised, giving the hacker control of approximately $5 million worth of ZK tokens — the remaining unclaimed tokens from the ZKsync airdrop. The ZKsync Security Council sent an onchain message to the hacker on Monday, April 21st at 15:03 UTC. In an effort to resolve this matter in the spirit of safe harbor, they offered a 10% bounty for returning 90% of the funds involved in the exploit. On Wednesday, April 23rd at 14:39 UTC, 90% of the funds were returned to the Era and Ethereum L1 addresses controlled by the Security Council.

In April 2025, a compromised admin key for three ZKsync airdrop Merkle distributor contracts enabled the unauthorized minting of 111 million ZK tokens, worth roughly $5 million. After incident response and negotiations, all funds were returned. A procedural failure left the admin of the ZKsync airdrop Merkle distributors controlled by a single-key multisig. This admin key was compromised, enabling the attacker to mint the remaining unclaimed tokens via the still-accessible sweepUnclaimed() function.

A compromised admin account exploited ZKsync's airdrop distribution contracts, minting approximately 111 million ZK tokens ($5 million) by calling a privileged sweep function. The loss was limited to unclaimed airdrop tokens and later fully recovered through a negotiated bounty. The airdrop distributor contracts used a single-signature admin multisig with no timelock or multi-party approval. When the admin key was compromised, the attacker could authorize sweepUnclaimed() calls and mint all unclaimed tokens without further security checks.
